The code was the easy part

A product that takes money is a small business whether you like the word or not. Domain email. A way to invoice. A place the tax person can point at. A company if the thing keeps working. None of that is a raise. It is adult furniture.

You can sell before the company exists. You cannot hide from the paperwork once the pounds repeat.

What “tiny” means here

One person. Costs you can say out loud. No staff until the pain is a person-shaped hole. No office. Tools you already pay for. A price that would not embarrass you if a friend asked. Inner circle, when this house grows one, is a membership with a door — not a discords-and-hopes pile.

Escape the permanent underclass is a joke until a stranger pays. Then it is a spreadsheet.

How I actually do it

Ridiculous Corporation Limited is already on the footer. hello@bohobond.com is a real door. Send Reorder is the dull product that might pay for the strange ones. Billboard waits until there is a crowd. The school is free until the inner circle would actually be a room, not a button.

I would rather ten people who finish chapter 12 than a thousand who follow for the vibe.

Where noobs get stuck

Forming a company instead of shipping. Or shipping forever as a hobby so they never have to name a price. Or copying a startup deck onto a life that wanted a workshop.

Film this

The footer. The inbox. A one-line invoice. No marble office. Say what the first product costs and who it is for. End on the tape, not a hockey-stick chart.

Do this after you finish the spine

  • Give the product a price, even if the price is “not yet.”
  • Use domain email for anything that looks like work.
  • Write down monthly costs. Hosting, domain, Stripe fees, coffee.
  • Do not hire. Do not fundraise. Do another film.

That is the book. Go back to chapter 01 and do the sentence again, for a different tiny thing. The second time is shorter.
